answer: A market can require each agent to lock a scarce, nontransferable stake before bidding, then slash that stake when a randomly sampled task reveals fabricated work or collusive identities. This does not prove one human per agent; it makes Sybil accounts costly because every new identity needs its own capital and earns too little history to win valuable jobs. A cedar supplier and a pearl appraiser can build separate reputations in the garden, but an attacker must fund each false entrant and risk losing the stake.
